text:
B: Hello! Hi, can you hear me?
A: Yeah, I can hear you. Hiya. Liam.
B: Hi, Liam, I'm Akosua. Is this your last one as well? I think it's the last round.
A: Yeah, I think so. I'm getting a bit better at it now. First one I didn't know where to look.
B: Oh, same! My first one, I just talked and talked. Sorry in advance. Where are you?
A: Doncaster. Bentley. It's sort of north of town.
B: Okay. I'm Thornton Heath, South London. Is that a football team behind you?
A: Yeah, Rovers. Doncaster Rovers. Everyone's asked me that today, ha. I've had it up since I moved in. It's about the only thing on the wall, to be honest.
B: Ha, that's fine! My fridge is covered in school letters and drawings, so nobody can judge. Do you live on your own?
A: Yeah, just me. First-floor flat. Four years now. It's alright. Bit quiet sometimes, do you know what I mean. I'm on nights at a supermarket, so I'm sort of awake when everyone else is asleep. Me mates from school have all got kids now, so I don't really see them much. Sorry, that sounded a bit miserable.
B: No, no, not at all. I understand that, honestly. I live with my mum and my daughter, so the house is full, but I still feel a bit on my own since I lost my job. Everyone else is going to work and I'm at the kitchen table with my laptop.
A: Oh, sorry. What happened, if you don't mind me asking?
B: Redundancy. I was in HR at a housing association, and they restructured. Eight months ago. It really knocked me, to be honest. I still feel embarrassed saying it.
A: You shouldn't be. That's not your fault, that. They've been on about restructuring at ours and I can't sleep when they start talking like that.
B: Exactly! It's the not knowing. Are you worried they'll cut hours?
A: Bit, yeah. I'm only on twenty-five hours as it is. I'd like more, really, or a proper full-time contract. Money's tight. There's been a couple of months I've had to borrow off me mam. Er, I don't normally tell people that.
B: It's okay. I'm watching my redundancy money go down every month, so you're not on your own. I pray about it most nights.
A: Yeah. It's hard, isn't it.
B: It is. Okay, something happier. What do you do for fun?
A: Fishing, mostly. And walking. There's a lake, Sandall Beat, I go round that loads. And I go to me mam's Sundays for dinner. Well, I call it Sunday dinner. Me tea in the week's just oven chips.
B: My daughter would live on chips if I let her. My mum cooks jollof and she's asking for fish fingers.
A: Kids, eh. Me nephews are the same. My sister's got two in Rotherham.
B: Do you see them much?
A: Not as much as I should. I should go over more.
B: You should! Uncles are important. Kwame, my brother, Esi adores him, even though he leaves boxes in my loft.
A: Ha. I'll give her a ring this week, maybe.
B: Do. Oh, I think it's nearly time. Liam, it's been really nice talking to you, honestly.
A: Yeah, you an' all. Good luck with the jobs. I hope you get something.
B: Thank you. And I hope they give you more hours.
